identification.summary: Moafee is a China-based cyber espionage group named by FireEye in September 2014 research that described it as operating from Guangdong Province and targeting military and government organizations involved in the South China Sea dispute [S1][S2][S3]. FireEye reported targets that included organizations within the US defense industrial base [S3]. FireEye described Moafee alongside a second group, DragonOK, which shares custom backdoors, RATs and the HTRAN proxy tool but was assessed as a distinct group with a different mission and location [S1][S3]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks Moafee as G0002 [S4].
identification.firstObserved: Publicly named by FireEye in September 2014 [S1][S2][S3]. The start date of its activity is not stated in the sources gathered.
identification.notes: Microsoft name: none found in the sources gathered. Cluster boundary: FireEye treats Moafee (Guangdong) and DragonOK (Jiangsu) as separate groups that may be subgroups with their own mission focus [S1][S3]. This encyclopedia's imported record merges DragonOK, BRONZE OVERBROOK and Shallow Taurus into Moafee; the sources gathered here describe DragonOK as a related but separate cluster, and no gathered source mapped BRONZE OVERBROOK or Shallow Taurus to either name. Post-2014 campaigns below are DragonOK reporting and are labeled as such. Press coverage spells the name variously as Moafee, Moafree and Moafe [S3].

attribution.confidence: FireEye assessed Moafee as a China-based group operating from Guangdong Province [S1][S2][S3]. No government attribution or named state sponsor appears in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: FireEye research released in September 2014 ahead of its full 'Operation Quantum Entanglement' report, as covered by trade press [S1][S2][S3]; MITRE ATT&CK group entry G0002 [S4].

objectives: Political and military espionage against government and military organizations with interests in the South China Sea dispute, per FireEye reporting [S2][S3]. FireEye contrasted this with DragonOK's economic espionage against high-tech and manufacturing companies [S1][S3].

targeting.notes: FireEye reported Moafee targets as military and government organizations involved in the South China Sea dispute, including organizations within the US defense industry [S2][S3]. Related cluster DragonOK targeted high-tech and manufacturing companies in Japan and Taiwan [S1][S2], and later Japan with possible targeting of Taiwan, Tibet and Russia [S6]. Specific Moafee victim countries are not named in the sources gathered.

capabilities.summary: FireEye reported that Moafee and DragonOK used similar TTPs, including custom-built backdoors and remote-administration tools, shared malware implants and social-engineering approaches, and the HTRAN proxy tool [S1][S2][S3]. MITRE ATT&CK notes binary padding for defense evasion and lists PoisonIvy among associated software [S4]. FireEye said the shared tooling may reflect collaboration, common training, a common toolkit supply chain, or a combination, and noted a possible third group using the same TTPs [S1][S3].

campaigns.name: Operation Quantum Entanglement (FireEye)
campaigns.summary: FireEye reported two China-based groups operating in parallel: Moafee, from Guangdong, targeting government and military organizations tied to the South China Sea dispute, including US defense industry targets, and DragonOK, from Jiangsu, targeting high-tech and manufacturing firms in Japan and Taiwan. Both used shared custom backdoors, RATs and HTRAN.

campaigns.name: DragonOK phishing against Japanese organizations (related cluster)
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 linked five phishing attacks against Japanese organizations between January and March 2015 to DragonOK. Each attack carried a Sysget (HelloBridge) variant, and the toolkit included a new backdoor, FormerFirstRAT, plus NFlog, PoisonIvy, NewCT and PlugX.

campaigns.name: DragonOK toolset update (related cluster)
campaigns.summary: Unit 42 reported new Sysget variants, along with IsSpace and TidePool, delivered by phishing and by RTF documents exploiting CVE-2015-1641. Japan remained the main focus, with possible targeting of Taiwan, Tibet and Russia.

diamond.adversary: China-based espionage operators that FireEye placed in Guangdong Province [S1][S3].
diamond.capability: Custom backdoors and RATs shared with DragonOK, the HTRAN proxy tool, PoisonIvy, and binary padding for evasion [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Proxied C2 using HTRAN [S2][S3]. No specific domains or IPs appear in the sources gathered.
diamond.victim: Government and military organizations involved in the South China Sea dispute, and US defense industrial base organizations [S2][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence on the South China Sea territorial dispute in support of Chinese interests, per FireEye's targeting description [S2][S3].
diamond.technology: Users' susceptibility to social engineering, and Windows hosts that run custom implants [S1][S4].

gaps: FireEye's 'Operation Quantum Entanglement' PDF could not be opened (WebFetch failed with DNS errors); details come from trade-press coverage of the research.
The MITRE ATT&CK G0002 page, the CFR Cyber Operations Tracker entry, the ETDA card and the Secureworks BRONZE OVERBROOK profile could not be fetched; their exact wording and dates are unverified.
No source gathered maps BRONZE OVERBROOK (Secureworks) or Shallow Taurus (Unit 42) to Moafee or to DragonOK; these imported aliases remain unverified.
No Microsoft name was found for Moafee or DragonOK.
No Moafee-specific activity after 2014 was found; all later reporting refers to DragonOK, a separate cluster per FireEye.
No government attribution or named state sponsor was found.
Specific Moafee victims, countries and infrastructure indicators are not public in the sources gathered.
The imported record cites a 2017 Phnom Penh Post report on new malware targeting Cambodia and a Morphick Rambo backdoor analysis; neither was verified here.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The relevant environment includes government, military and defense-industrial networks of South China Sea stakeholders, including US DIB contractors [S2][S3]. STEP 2: Spearphishing and custom RATs mean user mailboxes and endpoints are the primary avenues of approach [S1][S5]. STEP 3: The doctrinal template is socially engineered delivery, then a custom backdoor or PoisonIvy, with C2 relayed through HTRAN proxies [S1][S3][S4]. STEP 4: MLCOA is persistent collection of policy and military planning information related to South China Sea issues from government and DIB targets. MDCOA is coordinated collection across allied and partner networks during a maritime crisis, using shared toolkits that blur attribution between related clusters [S1][S3]. Candidate indicators: HTRAN proxy activity, PoisonIvy or NewCT-family implants, binary-padded executables, and themed phishing to personnel working on the South China Sea [S3][S4][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: shared tooling across Moafee, DragonOK and a possible third group means detections of these malware families should be correlated across clusters rather than assigned to one actor [S1][S3]. (2) Authorities: DIB targeting implies coordination with contractors under DIB cybersecurity information-sharing mechanisms [S3]. (3) Mission assurance: protect planning data on South China Sea and Indo-Pacific operations held on mission-partner networks [S2][S3]. (4) Coordination: regional partners named as DragonOK targets (Japan, Taiwan) may hold telemetry relevant to the shared toolkit [S1][S6].
